lessons.title: Introduction to Kinetic Art: History and Principles
lessons.body: Kinetic art is sculpture that moves. The movement can be powered by wind, motors, or people. In Africa, traditional kinetic art includes wind-driven mobiles made from palm fronds and seed pods, but modern metal kinetic sculpture uses bearings, gears, and motors. The principles are simple: a sculpture must be balanced, have a pivot or bearing, and a force to create motion. Start by studying simple wind spinners made from bicycle spokes and tin cans. You can make a basic spinner by cutting a plastic bottle into a spiral and mounting it on a nail. For metal, use 1mm to 2mm sheet metal, cut with tin snips, and bend with pliers. A common beginner project is a whirligig: a flat metal figure with a propeller. The propeller is cut from a 20cm x 20cm sheet, twisted 30 degrees, and mounted on a 6mm steel rod. The rod goes through a 6mm ID bronze bushing or a skateboard bearing. Test by blowing on it; it should spin freely. In Africa, you can source materials from scrap yards: car wheel bearings, bicycle axles, and washing machine motors. Remember, kinetic sculpture fails if friction is high or balance is off. Always test each moving part separately before assembling. For history, look at the windmills of ancient Persia and the mobile sculptures of Alexander Calder, but also local examples like the rotating weather vanes on church steeples in Cape Town. Your goal is to make movement that is reliable and visually interesting. Start with a simple spinning top made from a bolt and a nut welded to a rod. Spin it on a metal plate. If it wobbles, adjust the weight. This teaches balance. Then move to a horizontal axis: a metal fish that swings side to side on a pivot. Use a 10mm bolt as the pivot, with two nuts locked together to hold the fish. The fish should be cut from 2mm aluminium, 30cm long, and weighted at the tail with a 50g piece of lead. When pushed, it should swing 10 times before stopping. That is your first kinetic sculpture. Document each step with photos. In rural areas, you can use a charcoal forge to heat and bend metal. Always wear safety glasses and gloves. Kinetic art is about play and observation. Watch how a leaf falls, how a wheel turns. Then replicate that motion with metal.

lessons.title: Bearings, Pivots, and Rotational Movement
lessons.body: Bearings reduce friction and allow smooth rotation. Without them, your sculpture will grind and stop. The three main types for sculpture are: plain bearings (bushings), ball bearings, and roller bearings. For low-speed, low-load kinetic art, plain bearings are fine. Make a plain bearing from a bronze bushing or a piece of nylon. A 10mm steel shaft in a 10mm ID bronze bushing will spin freely if lubricated with a drop of engine oil. For higher loads, use ball bearings from skateboards (608ZZ, 8mm ID, 22mm OD, 7mm thick) or from car alternators. These are sealed and need no maintenance. In Africa, you can salvage bearings from dead washing machines, fans, and bicycles. A bicycle hub bearing is a cup-and-cone type; adjust it until there is no play but it still spins. For pivots, a simple bolt through a hole works, but it will wear. Better: use a shoulder bolt or a clevis pin. For a rotating sculpture on a vertical axis, use a thrust bearing. A cheap thrust bearing is a large washer between two smaller washers with grease. Or use a car wheel bearing, which handles both radial and thrust loads. Mount the bearing in a housing: weld a piece of pipe to your base, with an inner diameter matching the bearing OD. Press the bearing in with a hammer and a block of wood. The shaft should be a tight fit in the bearing inner race; if loose, use a punch to stake it or add a set screw. For horizontal axes, like a windmill, use two bearings spaced apart to prevent wobble. Align them by drilling both housing holes at once with a drill press or a hand drill guided by a jig. Misalignment causes binding. Test by spinning the shaft; it should coast for at least 5 seconds. If it stops quickly, ream the holes or add a shim. For very slow rotations, like a mobile, you can use a simple pivot: a nail through a hole with a small washer. But for anything over 100 RPM, use a ball bearing. Lubricate with lithium grease. In dusty environments, sealed bearings are best. Clean and repack bearings from scrap with new grease. A common mistake is to overtighten a pivot; leave a little play. Another is to use a bearing that is too small for the load; it will crush. Calculate load: a 1kg sculpture on a 8mm bearing is fine; a 10kg sculpture needs a 20mm bearing. Always test with a dummy load before final assembly. For rotational movement, the axis must be vertical or horizontal. Use a plumb bob to check vertical alignment. For horizontal, use a spirit level. If the axis is off by more than 2 degrees, the sculpture will wobble. Fix by adjusting the base or using shims. Remember, bearings are the heart of kinetic sculpture. Spend time getting them right.

lessons.title: Motors and Simple Mechanisms
lessons.body: Motors turn electricity into rotation. For kinetic sculpture, you need low-speed, high-torque motors. Good sources: microwave turntable motors (2-3 RPM, 220V AC), car windshield wiper motors (12V DC, high torque), and stepper motors from printers (need a driver). In Africa, you can salvage these from scrap. A microwave turntable motor is ideal for slow rotating displays. It runs on mains power, so be careful. Connect it with a plug and switch, and insulate all wires. For battery power, use a 12V wiper motor. It draws about 2-5 amps, so use a 12V 7Ah sealed lead-acid battery. To reduce speed, use pulleys: a 2cm pulley on the motor and a 10cm pulley on the shaft gives a 5:1 reduction, so a 100 RPM motor becomes 20 RPM. Belts can be rubber O-rings or V-belts from a sewing machine. For direct drive, couple the motor shaft to the sculpture shaft with a flexible coupling made from a piece of rubber hose and two hose clamps. This absorbs misalignment. For reciprocating motion (back and forth), use a crank and connecting rod. A crank is a disc with an offset pin. The connecting rod is a metal strip with holes at both ends. As the crank turns, the rod pushes and pulls. This is how a windshield wiper works. You can make a crank from a bicycle pedal arm. For oscillating motion, use a cam: a disc with a bump. A follower rides on the cam and moves up and down. Make a cam from a metal disc with a welded bolt. For intermittent motion, use a Geneva mechanism, but that is complex. Start with a simple motorized turntable: a microwave motor turning a 30cm metal disc. Weld a 6mm shaft to the disc, connect to the motor with a coupling. The disc should rotate at 2 RPM. Add a sculpture on top. For a more dynamic piece, use a wiper motor with a crank to move a metal bird's wings. The wings pivot on a 6mm bolt. The crank stroke should be 5cm. Use a 12V battery and a toggle switch. Test the mechanism without the sculpture first. Listen for binding. If the motor stalls, reduce load or increase voltage. Add a fuse (5A) to protect the motor. For outdoor sculptures, use a solar panel (10W) and a charge controller to charge a 12V battery. Then run the motor. In dusty conditions, cover the motor with a cloth or a metal shield. Lubricate moving parts with grease every month. Remember, motors can be dangerous: never touch moving parts, and keep wires away from water. Always disconnect power before adjusting. With a few salvaged motors, you can create endless motion.

lessons.title: Balancing and Counterweights
lessons.body: Balance is critical for kinetic sculpture. An unbalanced sculpture will wobble, wear out bearings, and stop. The center of gravity (CG) must be aligned with the pivot or axis of rotation. For a vertical axis, the CG should be directly above the pivot. For a horizontal axis, the CG should be below the pivot for stability (like a pendulum). To find the CG of a flat metal piece, balance it on a knife edge. Mark the line where it balances. Do this in two directions; the intersection is the CG. For a 3D piece, hang it from two points; the CG lies at the intersection of the plumb lines. Once you know the CG, you can add counterweights. A counterweight is a heavy mass on the opposite side of the pivot. For a wind sculpture that rotates, you want the CG at the axis. If the CG is off, add a weight (e.g., a stack of washers) on the light side. For a mobile, each arm must be balanced: the product of weight and distance on one side must equal the other. Example: a 100g weight 10cm from the pivot needs a 50g weight 20cm on the other side. Use a formula: W1 x D1 = W2 x D2. For a swinging pendulum, the CG should be below the pivot. If it's above, it will be unstable and flip. For a rotating sculpture on a horizontal axis, like a Ferris wheel, the CG should be at the center. Add weights to each arm to balance. In Africa, you can use scrap metal pieces as counterweights: old bolts, nuts, or lead fishing weights. For a large outdoor sculpture, use concrete blocks as counterweights. Always test balance by spinning the sculpture slowly by hand. It should come to rest at the same point each time if it's a pendulum, or spin freely if it's a rotor. If it stops at random, it's balanced. If it always stops at the same spot, that spot is heavy; add weight opposite. For a wind sculpture, balance is dynamic: the wind pushes on the blades, so the CG should be on the axis. Use a spirit level to check that the axis is vertical. For a hanging mobile, balance each level separately from the bottom up. Start with the lowest arm, balance it, then hang it on the next arm, and balance that. Use thin wire or fishing line for suspension. In dusty or windy conditions, add a small amount of weight to compensate for wind resistance. Remember, a well-balanced sculpture needs less power to move. It also lasts longer. Take time to balance: it's the difference between a frustrating failure and a mesmerizing success.

lessons.title: Wind and Solar Powered Movement
lessons.body: Wind and solar are free power sources for kinetic sculpture, ideal for outdoor installations in Africa where sunlight and wind are abundant. For wind, you need a rotor: a set of blades that catch the wind and spin a shaft. The simplest is a Savonius rotor: two half-cylinders (cut from a 200L drum) offset on a vertical axis. It spins in any wind direction. Cut a drum in half lengthwise, then cut each half to 1m tall. Weld them to a central 20mm shaft, with a 10cm gap between the two halves. Mount the shaft in two bearings (e.g., car wheel bearings) on a frame. The Savonius rotor starts in low wind (2 m/s) and produces high torque. For a horizontal-axis windmill, use a bicycle wheel with sheet metal blades. Cut 6 blades from 1mm aluminium, each 60cm x 15cm, twisted 20 degrees. Bolt them to the wheel spokes. The wheel spins a shaft via a pulley. For a decorative wind spinner, use a propeller from a small fan or make one from a plastic bottle. For solar, use a 10W to 50W photovoltaic panel. Connect it to a charge controller, then to a 12V battery (e.g., 7Ah to 100Ah). The battery powers a 12V motor (wiper motor or gear motor). A 10W panel can charge a 7Ah battery in about 8 hours of sun. Use a timer or a light sensor to turn the motor on at night or during the day. For a solar-powered rotating sculpture, use a 12V motor with a 100:1 gearbox. Connect the motor to a 30cm disc. The disc rotates once every 10 minutes. Add mirrors or reflective metal to catch the sun. In Africa, dust is a problem: clean solar panels weekly. For wind, use sealed bearings to keep out dust. For hybrid, combine wind and solar: a small wind turbine (100W) and a 50W panel charging the same battery. Use a blocking diode to prevent reverse flow. For a simple wind-powered kinetic sculpture, make a whirligig: a metal bird with a propeller on its back. The propeller spins a shaft that moves the bird's wings via a crank. Use a 20cm propeller, a 6mm shaft, and a crank with a 2cm stroke. The bird's body is a 2mm steel plate, 30cm long. The wings pivot on bolts. Test in a fan before outdoor installation. For solar, a simple project is a sun-tracking flower: a small solar panel on a motorized pivot that follows the sun. Use a light-dependent resistor (LDR) circuit to control the motor. This is more advanced but teaches electronics. Start with wind because it's mechanical and easier to repair. Always secure outdoor sculptures against strong winds: anchor the base with concrete or stakes. Use guy wires for tall pieces. In coastal areas, use stainless steel or galvanized metal to resist salt. With wind and solar, your sculpture can move forever, day and night.

lessons.title: Project: Kinetic Wind Sculpture
lessons.body: In this project, you will build a kinetic wind sculpture that spins and sways in the breeze. The design: a vertical axis wind spinner with three arms, each holding a curved metal sail. The arms rotate around a central shaft, and the sails are angled to catch the wind. Materials: 1.5m of 20mm steel pipe for the central shaft; two car wheel bearings (or 20mm ID pillow block bearings); 1m x 1m of 1mm galvanized sheet metal; 3m of 10mm steel rod for arms; 6 bolts (M10 x 50mm) with nuts; 1m of 25mm angle iron for the base; concrete for anchoring; paint. Tools: angle grinder with cutting and grinding discs, welding machine (or bolts if no welder), drill with 10mm bits, tin snips, hammer, pliers, measuring tape, spirit level, spanner. Steps: 1. Cut the central shaft to 1.2m. Weld a 10mm thick plate to the bottom to sit on the bearing. 2. Make the base: weld the angle iron into a cross shape, 60cm x 60cm. Drill holes for concrete anchors. 3. Mount the lower bearing in a housing welded to the base center. The shaft should fit through. 4. Mount the upper bearing 30cm above the lower bearing, held by three legs welded to the base. 5. Cut three arms from 10mm rod, each 50cm long. Weld them to the top of the shaft at 120 degrees apart, angled slightly upward (10 degrees). 6. Cut three sails from sheet metal: each 40cm x 30cm, curved by hammering over a pipe. 7. Bolt each sail to an arm using two M10 bolts, with the sail offset at 30 degrees to the arm. 8. Balance the rotor: spin it by hand. If it stops at the same point, weld a small weight (e.g., a nut) on the opposite arm. 9. Paint all metal with rust-resistant paint. 10. Dig a hole 40cm deep, place the base, and fill with concrete. Let cure for 48 hours. 11. Test: push the sails; the rotor should spin freely for at least 10 seconds. In wind, it should rotate continuously. Maintenance: grease bearings monthly; check bolts for tightness; touch up paint yearly. Safety: wear gloves and glasses when cutting and welding. This sculpture can be scaled up: for a 3m version, use 50mm shaft and larger bearings. For a more artistic look, cut the sails into leaf or bird shapes. Add a tail vane to keep it facing the wind if you use a horizontal axis. For a vertical axis, no tail needed. This project teaches bearings, balance, welding, and wind power. Once complete, you have a piece that moves with the wind, a mesmerizing addition to any garden or public space. Document your build with photos and share with rise AFRICA skills.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a bearing in kinetic sculpture?
options: B) To reduce friction and allow smooth rotation
quiz.explanation: Bearings reduce friction between moving parts, enabling smooth and efficient rotation.

quiz.q: Which material is commonly used for a plain bearing in low-speed kinetic art?
quiz.explanation: Bronze bushings are durable and provide low friction for low-speed applications.

quiz.q: What is the ideal type of bearing for a vertical axis sculpture that carries a heavy load?
quiz.explanation: A thrust bearing is designed to support axial loads, making it ideal for vertical axes with heavy loads.

quiz.q: How can you reduce the speed of a motor for a kinetic sculpture?
options: B) Use a pulley system with different sizes
quiz.explanation: A pulley system with a small pulley on the motor and a larger pulley on the output shaft reduces speed and increases torque.

quiz.q: What is a common source of a low-speed AC motor for kinetic sculpture?
quiz.explanation: Microwave turntable motors are low-speed (2-3 RPM) and easily salvaged.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a crank and connecting rod mechanism?
options: A) To convert rotary motion to reciprocating motion
quiz.explanation: A crank and connecting rod converts rotary motion into back-and-forth (reciprocating) motion.

quiz.q: How do you find the center of gravity of a flat metal piece?
options: B) By balancing it on a knife edge
quiz.explanation: Balancing on a knife edge in two directions locates the center of gravity at the intersection.

quiz.q: For a mobile, if you have a 100g weight 10cm from the pivot, what weight is needed 20cm on the other side to balance?
quiz.explanation: Using W1 x D1 = W2 x D2: 100g x 10cm = W2 x 20cm, so W2 = 50g.

quiz.q: Where should the center of gravity be for a swinging pendulum?
quiz.explanation: For stability, the center of gravity should be below the pivot so gravity restores it to the lowest point.

quiz.q: What is a Savonius rotor?
options: B) A vertical-axis wind turbine made from half-cylinders
quiz.explanation: A Savonius rotor is a vertical-axis wind turbine that uses two or more half-cylinders to catch wind from any direction.

quiz.q: What is the typical voltage of a car windshield wiper motor?
quiz.explanation: Most car wiper motors operate on 12V DC.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a charge controller in a solar-powered sculpture?
options: B) To prevent battery overcharge and overdischarge
C) To convert DC to AC
quiz.explanation: A charge controller regulates the voltage and current from the solar panel to protect the battery.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good counterweight material for a large outdoor sculpture?
quiz.explanation: Concrete blocks are heavy, weather-resistant, and inexpensive, making them ideal counterweights.

quiz.q: What is the recommended clearance between a shaft and a plain bearing for free rotation?
quiz.explanation: A clearance of about 0.1mm allows free rotation without excessive play.

quiz.q: How can you check if a bearing is properly aligned?
options: A) Spin the shaft; it should coast for at least 5 seconds
B) Hit it with a hammer
quiz.explanation: If aligned and not binding, the shaft should spin freely and coast for several seconds.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of using a sealed ball bearing in a dusty environment?
options: B) It keeps out dust and retains lubrication
D) It requires no maintenance ever
quiz.explanation: Sealed bearings have seals that prevent dust and moisture from entering, extending their life.

quiz.q: What is the typical speed of a microwave turntable motor?
quiz.explanation: Microwave turntable motors are designed for slow rotation, typically 2-3 revolutions per minute.

quiz.q: What is a Geneva mechanism used for?
quiz.explanation: A Geneva mechanism converts continuous rotation into intermittent rotary motion.

quiz.q: What is the first step in balancing a mobile?
options: A) Start from the top and work down
B) Start from the bottom and work up
C) Balance all arms at once
quiz.explanation: Balancing from the bottom up ensures each level is stable before adding the next.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a tail vane on a wind sculpture?
options: B) To keep the rotor facing the wind
quiz.explanation: A tail vane acts like a weather vane, pointing the rotor into the wind for maximum efficiency.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common mistake when mounting a bearing?
options: A) Using a bearing that is too large
quiz.explanation: Overtightening can crush the bearing or cause binding, leading to premature failure.

quiz.q: What is the recommended cure time for concrete anchoring a sculpture base?
quiz.explanation: Concrete typically reaches sufficient strength after 48 hours, though full cure takes longer.

quiz.q: What is the main function of a counterweight in a kinetic sculpture?
options: B) To balance the sculpture and reduce stress on bearings
quiz.explanation: Counterweights balance the sculpture, reducing vibration and wear on moving parts.

quiz.q: What is the typical power output of a small solar panel used for kinetic sculpture?
quiz.explanation: A 10W panel is common for small-scale projects, providing enough power to charge a small battery.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a fuse in a motor circuit?
options: B) To protect the motor from overcurrent
D) To convert AC to DC
quiz.explanation: A fuse melts and breaks the circuit if current exceeds a safe level, protecting the motor and wiring.

quiz.q: What is the best way to cut sheet metal for a kinetic sculpture?
options: B) With tin snips or an angle grinder
quiz.explanation: Tin snips are for thin sheets, while an angle grinder with a cutting disc is for thicker sheets.

quiz.q: What is the recommended angle for wind turbine blades to catch the wind efficiently?
quiz.explanation: A twist of about 20-30 degrees provides a good angle of attack for wind capture.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of a vertical-axis wind turbine over a horizontal-axis one?
options: B) It works in any wind direction
quiz.explanation: Vertical-axis turbines do not need to be pointed into the wind, so they work from any direction.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of painting a metal sculpture?
options: B) To protect against rust and corrosion
quiz.explanation: Paint provides a barrier against moisture and oxygen, preventing rust.

quiz.q: What should you do before adjusting a motorized sculpture?
quiz.explanation: Always disconnect power to prevent accidental startup and injury.
